To my knowledge, no calibration was performed for the transmitters before they were deployed. Can I perform any kind of opportunistic calibration using these values, other values provided by Argos that I have not listed, or calibration data from an unrelated project as a better-than-nothing measure? Thanks in advance, I am very new to spatial analysis and can use all the help I can get.

messages.body_plain:
Hello, apologies - I feel like all my questions are so basic but I really want to follow the process right.

Two unrelated questions:
1. Home range meta analysis - so I've produce AKDE home ranges for all of my animals. I subset each one from the master dataset and went through the home range estimation process for each one individually. I wasn't sure if I could have ran this from the master dataset but figured some might need different mitigation measures based on their data so I did each one independently. Now I'm working through the home range meta analysis process so I can compare between groups (e.g. age, region, habitat, etc) but noticed I need to use a consolidated dataset so that AKDE's are calculated on the same grid for all individuals. How then does this affect the nuance of the AKDE's calculated independently whereby different mitigation measures have been applied for certain individuals (e.g. bootstrapping for small sample sizes)? Wont combining them all and calculating AKDE's using a standard method produce different results?

2. Some of my AKDE's extend into the pacific ocean even though the species Im tracking is completely terrestrial albeit occupies near-coastal environments. Therefore I want to make the land mass a hard border in calculating AKDE's. So really just want to check that the way to do that is in the AKDE function using a shapefile of the landmass (i.e a SpatialPolygonsDataFrame) in the SP argument along with the SP.in = TRUE as I want the locations and home range to be inside its boundaries.

Thank you so much for the support in using this package and process.

Chris

Jesse

messages.subject_clean: Diffusion rate's relationship with different movement models
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Hopefully this is an easy one and I'm misunderstanding something. I have a question about diffusion rates produced in ctmm.

For context, I have a dataset comprised of 52 individuals GPS tracked before, during and after fire and I'm interested in seeing if fire led to an increase or decrease in diffusion rates. Fortunately, the species I'm working with had very fast range crossing times, so stationarity is easy to confirm and diffusion effective sample sizes are relatively large (often between 50 - 150) for each individual and time period.

I've used ctmm.select to fit movement models and whilst OUF or OUf was often selected, OU models were also supported in a reasonable number of individuals. The question I have is this: How much of a difference in diffusion rate estimates would I expect to see if these estimates were predicted from different movement models? Is it crucial to ensure any comparison of diffusion rates occurs only within predictions from the same movement model (OUF, OUf, OU etc)?

I'll have a play around with visualising estimates from each movement model type out of curiosity, but if you have any simple theoretical/practical guidance to give here, that would be very much appreciated!

Thanks,

Mark

messages.subject: Classified hunting locations and RSF
messages.body_plain:
Hello Group,

 We are trying to quantify which agricultural land cover
types barn owls are using.

Our current approach has been to classify and subset hunting
locations with the EMbC R package based on turning angles/velocity, then use the subset of only the hunting GPS
points in the CTMM pipeline, where we fit CTMMs, calculate AKDEs, and fit RSFs
using tracks of just the hunting GPS points.

 We realize this may not be the most conventional approach
and have a few questions regarding this method:

1) is this a valid approach to the RSF model using the ctmm
package?

2) is there a good way to validate this method?

3) Is there another approach to incorporate behavioral
classifications directly within the ctmm package that allows us to compare how
habitat preferences differ between hunting, commuting, and perching?

Thank you for your time,

Ryan

It makes sense to run AKDE on the winter ranges and the summer ranges separately.

It makes sense to run AKDE on a stopover site, if they stick around there for a little while, and you have multiple location fixes at that stopover site. And, so it makes sense to run AKDE on multiple stopover sites in the same way.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Lisa,

The CoV returned by meta() is that of the population of home-range areas, and will stabilize with more data. Is your CV target the coefficient of variation of the estimate of the population mean w.r.t. its sampling distribution? If so, that makes sense. It might be easier to look at the CI width divided by the point estimate. Asymptotically, that width should shrink with 1/sqrt(N). So if you set your target on that, then you can work out what N needs to be with some algebra. I get:

N <- N0 * ( (CI[3]-CI[1])/CI[2]/MAX.WIDTH )^2

where N0 is the initial number (14) and MAX.WIDTH could be something like 20% or something.

Best,
Chris
